justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish near-term outlook on what appears to be an asset trading around 408–412 at the time of forecasting. For the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the last observed price with a slight upward bias, reflecting typical short-term momentum and the assumption that no major catalysts were imminent. For the one-week estimate, I nudged the target slightly higher to 413, incorporating a mild continuation of any prevailing trend while acknowledging that weekly moves tend to revert somewhat toward recent averages. The one-month estimate of 418 reflects a more deliberate trend extrapolation, assuming gradual drift upward consistent with whatever medium-term directional bias existed at the time, while still remaining relatively conservative rather than projecting aggressive continuation.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect the natural scaling of uncertainty over time. At one day, a roughly 31-point range captures typical intraday-to-overnight volatility plus some tail risk from surprise news. By one week, that range expands to 56 points to account for multiple trading sessions, potential macro data releases, and the compounding of daily uncertainty. At one month, the 116-point interval reflects the reality that over four weeks, sentiment shifts, earnings, central bank communications, and global macro developments can produce substantial moves in either direction. The asymmetry in widths is roughly consistent with volatility scaling proportional to the square root of time, though I applied some additional discretionary widening for the monthly horizon given elevated macro uncertainty.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a surprise hawkish policy shift from a major central bank, an unexpected deterioration in economic data, or a geopolitical escalation could easily breach the lower bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon. A liquidity event or flash crash, while rare, could puncture even the one-day interval. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected economic print, a dovish policy surprise, or a broad risk-on rotation driven by resolution of an ongoing uncertainty could push prices well above 441 or even 476 within the stated timeframes. My intervals are meant to capture roughly 90% of likely outcomes, meaning by construction there remains a meaningful 10% probability of exceeding them in either direction, and fat-tailed financial markets make those tail events more common than a normal distribution would suggest.
